Phase 2 · Systems maps · October 28, 2026 · Data visualization and systems lead

Systems map directions

Dustin asked whether the studio can make a systems map that is distinct, visual, intuitive and beautiful, starting from scratch, with the current system kept if nothing gets there (G1-11). He asked one thing in particular: on the loop catalog, each loop should be a small copy of its own card, so R8 there is a miniature of the R8 card. This board shows the current system, seven explorations, three directions built from Atlas V7 by script, and a recommendation. Scope is a spec and specimens (G1-08); the working atlas file is untouched.

Recommendation: Orbit for the catalog and the loop cards, with Direction 3's fabric as the whole-system map. Every drawn ID, sign, grade, delay and reform target was checked against V7 by script.

Current systemFirst principlesExplorationsShared marks1 Orbit2 Line3 WeaveRecommendationReform viewPhoneChecksDecisions

Baseline

The current system

Concepts V2 is the system Dustin likes and the fallback if no direction gets there (G1-11). Its loop catalog draws its 20 numbered loops on one ring and leaves the 3 sketched loops out, so a two-step loop and a four-step loop look alike and the plate reads as one ring repeated. Its R8 card is the drawing Dustin singled out: two boxes, a step named in words, a return line underneath. Both came before Gate 1, so they still use board-written short names and the plain grade words ("some evidence") that Gate 1 replaced with V7's words (M2).

What it does well

One quiet vocabulary across every view. The read-aloud sentence. The return line, which shows in one glance that a loop comes back. Area cards on the circuit that a newcomer can name.

What this pass has to beat

A catalog where every loop looks the same, so the page cannot show which loops are long, slow or uncertain. A whole-system map that groups wires by area, so no single connection can be followed. Grade words and short names that predate Gate 1.

First principles

Who reads a systems map, and what they need in ten seconds

The reader

A first-time reader anywhere in the country, of any party, who came for one rule that touches their week: a rent notice, a primary ballot, a power bill. They have never seen a causal loop diagram. They will give a figure ten seconds before deciding whether it is for them.

What each view must show in ten seconds

  1. Whether the loop feeds itself or pushes back.
  2. Which step is weakest, meaning the least certain.
  3. Where a reform can act.
  4. How slowly it turns.

The model never adds reform effects into a score or estimates how strong a whole loop is, so no view may suggest either.

The four views

  1. Loop catalog: all 23 loops at once, each a miniature of its own card.
  2. Loop card: one loop in full. R8 is the worked example.
  3. Whole-system map: 51 variables and 118 connections, for orientation.
  4. Reform view: one reform's targets, red where it acts.

What the data holds

23 loops. 20 have numbered chains: 11 of two steps, 5 of three and 4 of four; 3 are sketched with no numbered chain. 18 reinforcing, 5 balancing. Every step carries a sign, a type, a delay class and an evidence grade. 46 of the 118 connections sit on a named loop.

Quirks the drawings work around

  • Three loops (B2, B3, R9) have no numbered chain, and two (R2, R16) close through a hypothesized step. Each says so in words, and sketched steps take the hollow line.
  • B2 to B5 name both a variable and a loop, so every loop ID sits in a typed chip (M3) and variables never do.
  • Grades are spelled several ways (V7.1 issue 1). The drawings read links[].evidence only and print V7's words.
  • Delay and effect codes share S, M and L (issue 22), so no bare letter appears outside a data table.
  • V7 never defines its spine flag, so no drawing encodes it.
  • Loops share connections: L42 sits on three. The fabric weaves a shared connection into each loop's band and marks the copies.

Explore widely, then choose

Seven form families on real loops

Each sketch is drawn by script from V7, mostly on Loop R8 (two slow, well-supported steps) and Loop R10 (four steps, from documented to plausible). The research brief (work/research/20261028_Systems-Map-References.md) shaped the choice: fixed positions and focus with context beat force layouts, a Sankey cannot carry a cycle, and bundles hide which line goes where.

Shared marks

One vocabulary under all three directions

Every direction draws with the Gate 1 marks (M1 to M4) exactly as approved: V7's line code with the record square and the hollow line, V7's grade words with their glosses, typed chips, the effect pips and the delay ticks. Four studio additions appear below them, each flagged in the decisions: the delay bow (Orbit only), the sign label at its smallest, the reform pointer and the loop-kind arrow. No drawing contains the ampersand or calls a shared variable a hinge, so the five separation rules hold.

Documented or well supported: a solid line (V7). Documented adds the record square to the label, Mark 1.

Plausible: dashed, V7's 9 4.

Contested: dash-dot, V7's 9 3 2 3. Credible studies disagree.

Hypothesis: dotted, V7's 2 4. Proposed, not yet supported.

A step in a sketched loop, which has no numbered connection: the hollow line, Mark 1.

Delay ticks at the start of a step: one under 2 years, two 2 to 10 years, three over 10 years, Mark 4.

The step's label at its smallest: its sign, with the record square when documented. A plus means the two move the same way, not that the change is good.

on the catalogon a card that names one reform

A reform acts here. Ink on the catalog, which names no single reform; Pillar Red on White where the view names one reform (Rule 05.3).

Loop kind, in the causal loop diagram convention: R feeds itself, B pushes back. Always printed with the words.

Direction 1

Orbit: each loop draws its own shape

A loop is a closed figure that comes back around. Each step bows outward by its delay, so a slow loop is round and a fast one is thin, and the catalog becomes 23 different drawings that a reader can tell apart at a glance.

Spec

Idea
A loop is a closed figure. A slow step takes the long way round, so every loop draws its own shape.
Grid and scale
Stations on a base circle, step 1 at twelve o'clock, clockwise, evenly spaced. Each step is a circular arc whose bow is a share of its chord: 0.14 under 2 years, 0.27 for 2 to 10 years, 0.42 over 10 years. The catalog uses a 58 to 62 px radius in a 236 by 206 cell; the card uses 178 px; the phone card 104 px. Only geometry scales.
Nodes and lines
Variables are Charcoal discs with the ID in Newsprint, 13 px (catalog) and 18 px (card). Lines 2 px (catalog), 2.5 px (card), in V7's texture; arrowheads 9 by 4.5; ticks 1.5 by 10 px. A sketched loop sits on the plain base circle in the hollow line.
Type
Inter 13 px bold for IDs and labels in the catalog, Inter 15 px semibold for step names on the card, Inter Tight 800 for card IDs and headlines. Nothing under 13 px.
Color
Charcoal for every data mark on Newsprint. Stone for context only. Red on the card and reform views only, on White, at the targets of the one reform the headline names.
Labels
Catalog: IDs, sign labels, the word 'weakest', pointers. Card: each step's ID, V7 name, grade and delay outside its arc, away from the center; station names outside the disc.
Scale
Miniature, card and phone card call one geometry function at three radii. The whole map keeps the rule (bend left, slower bends more) on one ring of all 51 variables.
Phone
Catalog as a list, miniature at 132 px beside its title. Card stacks: drawing at 326 px with IDs only, then the steps as a numbered list.

Loop catalog: all 23 loops, each drawn from its own steps

Catalog view, Newsprint, ink only. The catalog names no single reform, so it carries no working red (Rule 05.3); ink pointers show where each loop's own reforms act. Groups follow the area holding most of a loop's variables, with ties going to the area first in V7's order.

Loop card, full size

LoopR8Reinforcing loop: feeds itself. Closed: every step is a numbered connection.

Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building

Read it aloud: Housing scarcity raises homeowners' equity, which raises housing scarcity.

One turn takes
Over 10 years. V7 gives a loop the delay of its slowest step, and both steps here take over 10 years.
Weakest step
No single step. Both steps are graded well supported. V7's summary still calls L39 "the weaker step because equity is one motive among several for opposing construction."
Now
Running up. V7 tracks it by "Owner-renter net worth gap (SCF) 1989 to 2022".
Revised in V7
The loop grade note reads "well-supported for both links; the loop no longer depends on A1". The loop follows owners' equity and the gap between owners and renters. Rising home equity tends to lower the top 1% share of wealth (T12: Rising home equity lowers the top wealth share), so this loop does not explain that share.

Where a reform acts

ReformR-30 More homes allowed by right near jobs

Red marks where R-30 acts in this loop: L39, Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing; A5, Housing scarcity. It also acts outside this loop on LE17, Housing scarcity raises rents and prices. Reform R-06 also acts on L39; V7 does not list it on this loop.

Evidence that the problem exists: Well supported. Evidence that the remedy works: Plausible. Confidence in the effects, in V7's words: "high where binding; medium for US statutes".

Whole-system map

Direction 2

Line: ride each loop out and back

A loop is a line with stations in V7's chain order and a return line underneath, the strip map above a train door. It reads left to right like the loop's own sentence, and it grows from the R8 card Dustin singled out.

Spec

Idea
A loop is a line you ride out and back: stations in V7's chain order, the closing step on a return line underneath.
Grid and scale
Stations at a fixed pitch, 82 px in the catalog and 596 px between box centers on a two-step card, so a longer strip means more steps and nothing else. The return line drops 40 px (catalog) or 96 px (card) and runs back with 10 or 16 px corners.
Nodes and lines
Catalog stations are 30 by 22 Charcoal tiles with the ID. Card stations are boxes with a 6 px Charcoal spine, the ID, V7's chain label and its reading rule ('Higher: ...'). Lines and marks as Orbit.
Type
Inter 13 px in the catalog; 15 px semibold step names and 16 px bold station names on the card.
Color
As Orbit. Red marks the targeted step's whole line and the targeted station's outline.
Labels
Step names above each forward step, grade and delay below. The return step is labeled under the return line.
Scale
One function draws the strip at two pitches. The whole map lays all 51 variables on one line, drivers and the two lower layers first, then A to E; links that run right arc over, links that run back arc under.
Phone
The strip turns vertical: stations stacked, steps running down, the return line up the left side.

Whole-system map

Direction 3

Weave: each loop is a stitch in the fabric

Rows are variables and vertical threads are connections, after BioFabric. A loop is a run of threads that leaves a row and comes back to it, so every loop is a small stitch, and the whole system becomes a fabric with no crossing lines at all.

Spec

Idea
A loop is a stitch in the fabric of the system: rows are variables, vertical threads are connections.
Grid and scale
Rows in V7's system order, 44 px apart in the catalog and 86 px on the card, with an 18 or 34 px gap where the loop crosses into another area. One thread per step, in chain order, 60 or 150 px apart.
Nodes and lines
A dot where a thread leaves its row, an arrowhead where it lands. Row IDs in Charcoal tiles. Labels sit beside each thread so the texture stays visible.
Type
Inter 13 px for IDs and labels; card row names 16 px bold with the reading rule in 13 px.
Color
As Orbit. On the card, the loop's other connections to the rest of the system are Stone.
Labels
Card: each thread's ID, V7 name, grade and delay beside it; 'Its other connections' names the far variable at each stub.
Scale
The miniature is the card's rows and threads without names. The whole map is the full fabric: 51 rows, one band per numbered loop, then the connections on no loop.
Phone
Rows keep their names on the left; threads stay vertical, so the fabric scrolls down the screen.

Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building

One turn takes
Over 10 years. V7 gives a loop the delay of its slowest step, and both steps here take over 10 years.

Running up. V7 tracks it by "Owner-renter net worth gap (SCF) 1989 to 2022".

The loop grade note reads "well-supported for both links; the loop no longer depends on A1". The loop follows owners' equity and the gap between owners and renters. Whole-system map

Recommendation

Orbit for the loops, the fabric for the whole system

Orbit is the direction that gets there. It answers the ask exactly: on the catalog, R8 is a small copy of the R8 card, and the page holds 23 loops that each look like themselves, with the slow ones round and the fast ones thin. Its ring map is the one weak view, so the recommendation takes the fabric from Direction 3 as the whole-system map. Both use the same Gate 1 marks, so the reader learns one vocabulary.

Rubric, Master Brief V2 section 6, scored 1 to 5 by the studio (a design judgment); ship threshold 4 on every criterion
OptionCraftClarityBrand fidelityUsefulnessEvidence honestyAccessibilityReason
Current system (Concepts V2)444333Fine drawing and one calm vocabulary. The uniform catalog hides structure; pre-Gate 1 grade words and board-written short names; not rechecked at 390 px in this pass.
Direction 1, Orbit, as built434454The strongest catalog and an elegant card. The ring map shows the story (returns cross the middle) and stays busy along the rim: Clarity 3.
Direction 2, Line444454The most readable strip and card, closest to the R8 card Dustin likes. Least distinct from the current system, and its arc map fans out at the hub variables.
Direction 3, Weave433454The calmest, most legible whole map, and the only one with no crossings at all. Its miniatures read as notation before they read as loops.
Recommended: Orbit loops with the fabric map444454Orbit's catalog and cards with Weave's fabric as the whole-system map. Every criterion at 4 or above; the fabric needs a one-line reading guide and a guided first loop.

What it costs

  • Four new marks need Dustin's approval beside M1 to M4, which stay as approved: the delay bow, the sign label at its smallest, the reform pointer and the loop-kind arrow.
  • Readers learn one new sentence: "the slower the step, the wider it bows." The ticks still carry delay, so the bow adds a second channel and replaces none.
  • It gives up the research brief's first idea, one identical ring for every loop, in favor of Dustin's ask for loops that look different.
  • The fabric reads as notation at first sight. It needs its reading line, a guided first loop (R8), and focus with context in the live atlas.
  • Build: the atlas renderer needs two computed layouts (orbit geometry and the fabric order), both generated from V7 with no hand placement, so upkeep stays low.

What it keeps from the current system

  • The read-aloud sentence on every card.
  • The return idea: on the fabric, a loop's band shows it leaving a row and coming back.
  • V7's line code, the record square, the hollow line, the ticks, the typed chips and the effect pips, unchanged.
  • Red only where one reform acts, on White.

Which directionOrbit loops with the fabric map; Orbit with its own ring map; Line; Weave; the current system (G1-11 fallback)Orbit loops with the fabric mapIt answers the catalog ask, scores 4 or above on every criterion, and keeps M1 to M4 as approved.
The delay bow, a second delay channel beside the ticksAdopt; ticks onlyAdoptIt is what makes the 23 miniatures differ, and it says 'slow' without a number.
Three new marks: the sign label at its smallest, the reform pointer, the loop-kind arrowAdopt all three; adopt some; keep the Gate 1 set onlyAdopt all threeEach solves a ten-second task at catalog size where the Gate 1 labels do not fit.
Red on the catalogNone, ink pointers only; a reform filter that turns one reform's targets redNone by default, the filter in the live atlasThe catalog names no single reform, so under Rule 05.3 it carries no working red until a reader picks one.
The surface for views that carry redWhite; Newsprint with a Charcoal edge on redWhitePillar Red on Newsprint measures 2.96:1, and an edged red line looks like the hollow line for sketched steps.
The weakest-step ruleLowest V7 rank, ties shown as ties, V7's prose quoted on the card; V7's prose onlyLowest V7 rank, with the proseIt is computable for every loop, and the card still carries V7's reasons, as for R8's L39.

Red on this board follows Rule 05.3, quoted here word for word from D2-01: "The wordmark's ampersand and the lockmark's lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon's red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline's ampersand uses the view's working red. The hinge divider's ampersand takes its surface's ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian." The specimens on this board are specimens, so the board as a whole is not one view; inside each specimen, only one reform's targets take red.
